lesson.title: When Atoms Trade Electrons: Ionic Bonds and the Chemistry of Nerve Signals
lesson.summary: This section explains how ionic bonds form through the complete transfer of electrons between atoms, using table salt as a model case, and connects ionic bonding to the electrolyte gradients that power nerve impulses in animals.
lesson.body:
An ionic bond forms when one atom transfers one or more electrons completely to another atom, rather than sharing them, and the two resulting ions, now carrying opposite electrical charges, attract each other. This transfer happens because some atoms hold their valence electrons loosely, needing to lose only one or two electrons to reach a full, stable outer shell, while other atoms hold their valence electrons tightly and need to gain only one or two electrons to reach that same stable state. When such atoms meet, the electron rich atom accepts electrons from the electron poor atom rather than the two atoms splitting the difference.

The textbook example is table salt, sodium chloride. A sodium atom has a single electron in its outermost shell, and it is energetically favorable for sodium to lose that one electron rather than gain seven more to fill the shell. A chlorine atom, by contrast, has seven electrons in its outermost shell and needs only one more to complete it. When sodium and chlorine react, sodium donates its lone outer electron to chlorine. Sodium becomes a positively charged ion, written Na+, because it now has one more proton than electrons, while chlorine becomes a negatively charged ion, written Cl-, because it now has one more electron than protons. These oppositely charged ions attract each other electrostatically, and in solid table salt this attraction extends in a repeating three dimensional lattice rather than a single isolated pair, which is why salt crystallizes into the cubic shape visible even to the naked eye.

Ionic bonds matter to living organisms well beyond salt crystals, and one of the clearest examples is the electrical signaling system used by nerve cells throughout the animal kingdom. Nerve cells maintain very different concentrations of sodium ions and potassium ions, K+, inside versus outside the cell, a gradient actively maintained by a membrane protein called the sodium potassium pump. Because these ions carry electrical charge, moving them across the cell membrane changes the voltage across that membrane. A nerve impulse, or action potential, is essentially a rapid, traveling wave of ion movement: channels open that let sodium ions rush into the cell, briefly reversing the membrane's charge, and this change triggers neighboring channels further along the cell to open in turn, propagating the signal down the length of the neuron. None of this would work if sodium and potassium did not exist as freely dissolved, independently charged ions, a direct consequence of the same complete electron transfer that defines ionic bonding in solid salt.

It is worth noting an important difference between ionic bonds in a dry solid and ionic interactions in the watery environment of a living cell. In water, the strong attraction between water molecules and individual ions, which will make more sense once water polarity is covered later in this chapter, is often strong enough to pull ionic compounds apart entirely, a process called dissociation, so that sodium and chloride ions float independently rather than staying locked in a rigid lattice. This is precisely why salt dissolves in water and why ions like sodium and potassium can move freely through the fluid inside and outside living cells, an essential requirement for the nerve signaling example described above.
